messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame Mensah was 37 when he finally sought treatment, a single Black man who had spent years helping other people name and survive what frightened them. He worked as a psychologist in a community mental health clinic, and part of what made his own assault so disorienting was that it happened in a place that should have been ordinary. After staying late one evening for paperwork, he was cornered and raped by a man he knew professionally in a small office that locked from the inside. What remained with him most sharply was not only the assault itself but the trapped feeling of hearing the lock click, realizing the door would not open, and being forced to endure the presence of another man in close quarters while his own body stopped feeling like it belonged to him. Later, even passing remarks about sexual violence in trainings or case discussions could throw him back into that room, because the language landed with the same invasive force as the experience it named.

In the weeks after, Kwame did not talk about what had happened. He had come to believe that something fundamental had changed in how he appeared to other people, as if the assault had marked him in a visible way. Sitting with colleagues, he found himself certain they could see it just by looking at him. He also felt newly convinced that bad things could happen without warning and that he would be powerless to stop them. Those beliefs did not stay abstract. Because he felt exposed and helpless, being alone with men became charged almost immediately; an ordinary moment with a male coworker in a consultation room no longer felt neutral. The same was true of confined spaces. A closed office door, even in his own workplace, seemed to carry the meaning that he could be trapped again.

That sense of permanent vulnerability began to shape his body and his attention. In sessions he started choosing the chair with his back to the wall, scanning the room so he could see the door and whoever entered. If he had to meet with a male patient or a male colleague, he positioned himself carefully and stayed braced through the entire interaction. At night he struggled to fall asleep because lying down and letting go felt dangerous; he told himself he needed to stay alert, even in his apartment with the door locked. He could not relax in places he knew were objectively safe. What frightened him most was the feeling that safety no longer counted for much, because he was sure he could not stop another violation if it came. The more he lived in that state of readiness, the more hopeless he became about the future, as if this watchfulness was now the only way he could exist.

His work environment kept pressing on the same injuries. In case conference, if a trainee mentioned sexual assault, Kwame felt a jolt of dread before he had fully registered the words. He became acutely aware of the men in the room and of whether the door was shut. When an office door clicked closed during supervision, he would feel his body tense and his mind race ahead to danger. His constant vigilance made these moments harder, not easier; because he was already scanning for threat, comments about sexual violence, locked rooms, and being alone with men stood out immediately and hit with full force. By then he was no longer reacting only to reminders of the assault itself but to the whole network of conditions his mind had learned to treat as warnings.

Over time the vigilance and the bleakness fed each other. Each night spent awake, listening for sounds in the hallway, left him more certain that his life had narrowed into mere survival. Each day spent arranging chairs, monitoring exits, and enduring the strain of one-on-one meetings with men deepened his conviction that he was helpless and visibly damaged. He began to think, with increasing certainty, that he had no future beyond managing the next threat. Even when nothing happened, the fact that he could not stand down seemed like proof that the world was unsafe and that he had been altered beyond repair.

He came to treatment after nearly walking out of a multidisciplinary meeting when a male physician casually referenced a case of sexual violence and another staff member shut the conference room door. Kwame felt trapped, exposed, and suddenly sure everyone could see what had been done to him. He was shaken by how quickly he lost his sense of the present and by the realization that his professional world had become organized around avoiding the next moment of danger. What he fears most is that this is permanent—that he will never again sit in a room, close his eyes to sleep, or be alone with another man without feeling at risk. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that he might someday stop living as if the lock is always about to click.
